title: How to Build a Daily IELTS Study Habit Around Work or Classes
excerpt: You do not need four free hours a day. A small, fixed routine that survives long commutes and tired evenings will do more than a perfect plan you abandon by Thursday.
body:
Most of us start IELTS preparation with a big promise: three hours every evening. By the second week, the office runs late, the Dhaka traffic eats the evening, or a class assignment lands, and the promise breaks. Then we feel behind, and feeling behind makes the next session even harder to start.

The fix is not more willpower. It is a smaller, more stubborn routine. A habit that survives a bad day is worth more than a plan that only works on a good one.

## Start with the minimum, not the ideal

Pick a daily floor you can hit even when you are exhausted. For many learners that is 30 minutes. Write it down as your non-negotiable. Anything beyond that is a bonus, not an obligation.

On busy days the floor protects the chain. On free days you can do more, and the extra work feels like a gift rather than a debt.

## Attach study to something that already happens

Habits stick when they hang on an existing anchor. Think about what you already do every day without deciding to:

- The bus or metro ride: Listening practice, shadowing a recording, or reviewing vocabulary notes.
- The first cup of tea: one short Reading passage or 10 minutes of Writing planning.
- Dinner finished: a timed task or an error-log update.
- The lunch break at work: a few Speaking questions answered aloud, even quietly in a corner.

Match the task to the energy of the moment. Listening and vocabulary suit a tired commute. Writing and full Reading passages need a clear head, so give them your best slot.

## Plan for load-shedding and bad days

Power cuts and weak internet are part of life here, so build a backup. Keep an offline option ready: a printed passage, a downloaded audio file, a notebook for hand-written paragraph plans. Charge your phone and earphones before the evening, not during it.

Decide in advance what a rescue session looks like. For example: ten minutes of vocabulary and one speaking answer recorded on your phone. It is small, but it keeps the habit alive.

## Make the start easy

The hardest minute is the first one. Reduce friction:

- Leave your notebook and pen where you will sit.
- Keep one folder for today's task so you do not choose from a menu.
- Decide tomorrow's task before you finish today's.

When the next task is already chosen, you spend your energy studying rather than deciding.

## Track the streak, but forgive the gap

A simple calendar with a tick for each day works well. Seeing the chain is motivating. But missing one day should not mean quitting. A useful rule is never miss twice: if Tuesday goes wrong, Wednesday gets the floor session, no matter what.

Also watch for the opposite trap: studying every day but only doing the comfortable skill. If you love Reading and avoid Writing, the habit is healthy but the plan is lopsided. Rotate skills across the week so the weak one gets regular contact.

## Tell someone

A friend, a sibling, or a classmate preparing for the same test can keep you honest. A one-line message each night, such as "done, 35 minutes, Listening", is enough. Accountability does not need to be dramatic.

## What to expect

Habits take time to feel natural, and no routine can promise a particular band score. What it can give you is steady exposure to the test format, a growing record of what you have practised, and fewer evenings spent wondering whether you should study.

Try this week: choose your daily floor (we suggest 30 minutes), pick one anchor in your day to attach it to, and tick a calendar for seven days. If you miss a day, apply the never-miss-twice rule and carry on.

title: Why You Should Keep an Error Log, and How to Do It
excerpt: Practising more is not the same as improving. An error log turns every wrong answer into a pattern you can actually fix.
body:
Many learners finish a practice test, check the score, feel good or bad for a few minutes, and move on to the next test. The score tells you where you are, but it says very little about why. The real learning sits in the mistakes, and without a record those mistakes quietly repeat.

An error log is simply a notebook or spreadsheet where you write down what went wrong and why. It takes ten minutes after a practice session, and it is one of the most useful habits we can build.

## Why it works

Without a log, every wrong answer feels like a one-off. With a log, patterns appear. You may discover that most of your lost marks in Reading are True/False/Not Given questions, or that you keep missing plural endings in Listening, or that your Writing Task 2 paragraphs drift away from the question.

Once you can name a pattern, you can practise against it. Practising a named weakness is far more efficient than doing another random test.

## What to record

Keep each entry short. Useful columns are:

- Date and source: for example, Cambridge Reading, Test 3, Passage 2.
- Question type: matching headings, sentence completion, map labelling, and so on.
- Your answer and the correct answer.
- Cause of the error: this is the most important column.
- Fix: one concrete action for next time.

## Find the real cause

Be honest about why you were wrong. Common causes include:

- Vocabulary: you did not know a word or a paraphrase.
- Spelling or grammar: you heard or found the answer but wrote it incorrectly.
- Instructions: you ignored the word limit, such as no more than two words.
- Timing: you ran out of time or rushed the last passage.
- Concentration: you lost the thread in the audio.
- Strategy: you read the whole passage first when the question type needed scanning.

Careful here. "Careless mistake" is not a cause, it is a label that hides one. Ask what kind of carelessness: skipping the instructions, mishearing, or misreading a negative.

## Include Writing and Speaking

The log is not only for Reading and Listening. For Writing, note feedback patterns: weak paragraph structure, repeated vocabulary, article errors, tense slips, or a Task 1 overview that is missing. For Speaking, record questions where you froze, words you mispronounced, or answers that stopped after one sentence. Remember that Task 2 counts double in Writing, so recurring Task 2 issues deserve extra attention.

## Review it weekly

A log you never reread is just a diary. Set a fixed time each week, perhaps Friday evening, to count the causes. Circle the top two. Those become next week's practice targets. If vocabulary is the leader, spend short daily sessions on the paraphrases you missed. If spelling is the leader, build a personal list of the words you misspelt and test yourself on it.

Cross out entries once you have not repeated that error for a few weeks. Watching the list shrink is encouraging.

## Keep it light

If the log takes an hour, you will stop. A handwritten notebook is fine, and so is a phone note, which is handy when the power is out. Aim for quick, honest entries rather than neat ones.

Try this week: after your next practice section, write down every wrong answer with its cause and one fix. At the end of the week, count which cause appears most often and plan two short sessions against it.

title: How to Use Cambridge-Style Practice Tests Without Burning Them
excerpt: Real practice tests are limited, so every one should teach you something. Here is how to space them, review them, and still keep a few fresh for later.
body:
A set of Cambridge-style tests feels like a large library until you start to use it. Do two tests a day for a fortnight and suddenly the shelf is empty, your scores have barely moved, and you have nothing fresh left for the weeks before your exam.

Full tests are valuable because they are close to the real thing. That is exactly why we should spend them carefully.

## Do not start with full tests

Many learners begin with a full test to see their level. One early baseline is sensible. After that, a full test is not the best tool for building skills. If you are weak at matching headings or at following a map in Listening, a full test mixes everything together and hides the problem.

Question-type practice and single sections are better for early weeks. Save full tests for when you are ready to check timing and stamina.

## Treat each test as three uses

A well-used test can serve you more than once.

- First attempt: timed, under test conditions, with no pausing and no dictionary. Reading is 60 minutes for 40 questions, and Listening runs about 30 minutes for 40 questions.
- Review: mark it, then study every error and every lucky guess. Log the causes.
- Second pass: some days later, redo only the passages or sections where you struggled, or reread the transcript and shadow the audio. You are not chasing a higher number, you are learning the language and tricks in the test.

A single test used this way can fill several study sessions.

## Keep some tests untouched

Decide in advance how many tests stay sealed. A simple plan is to divide your available material into three groups:

- Training material: used for untimed or partly timed practice and reviewed deeply.
- Checkpoint tests: taken under full conditions every two to three weeks.
- Reserve tests: kept fresh for the final two weeks before the exam.

Mark the reserve tests clearly so you do not open one by accident on a bored evening.

## Make test conditions honest

A practice score only means something if the conditions were fair. Sit at a desk. Turn off notifications. Use the real time limit. Write your Reading and Listening answers directly, and in Writing stay within the time for each task, remembering Task 1 needs at least 150 words and Task 2 at least 250. If the power goes out mid-test, note it and retake that section later rather than guessing.

## Writing and Speaking need feedback

You can mark Listening and Reading yourself with an answer key. Writing and Speaking are different, because a practice response without feedback teaches little. Rather than writing many essays, write fewer and get each one reviewed against the IELTS criteria, then rewrite the weakest paragraph. For Speaking, record yourself, listen back, and compare it with the Part 1, 2 and 3 format.

## Do not chase scores

Scores on practice tests jump around, especially across different Reading passages. Look at trends over three or four tests rather than a single result, and read the error log for the reason behind each dip. No practice score can promise what you will get on exam day.

Try this week: sort your available tests into training, checkpoint, and reserve groups. Then take one section from the training pile, review it fully, and redo the hardest part three days later.

title: How to Plan a Weekly IELTS Study Schedule That You Can Actually Keep
excerpt: A good weekly plan balances all four skills, leaves room for review, and bends when real life gets in the way.
body:
Most study timetables fail for a boring reason: they were written for an imaginary person with no job, no family duties, and no power cuts. A schedule that works has to be built around the week you really live.

Here is a simple way to plan one, step by step.

## Step 1: Count your real hours

Take a sheet of paper and mark the fixed parts of your week: work or class hours, commute, prayer times, meals, family commitments. Be honest about tiredness, too. After a long day in Dhaka traffic, a full Writing essay may not happen.

What is left is your true study time. Many working learners find they have about one to two hours on weekdays and a bigger block at the weekend. That is enough to make progress if it is used well.

## Step 2: Give each skill a place

The four skills do not need equal time every day, but none should vanish for the week. A sample pattern for someone with an hour or so on weekdays:

- Sunday: Reading passages, timed, and a review of errors.
- Monday: Listening section plus vocabulary from the passages.
- Tuesday: Writing Task 1 practice, with a rewrite of last week's weak paragraph.
- Wednesday: Speaking practice, recorded and replayed.
- Thursday: Writing Task 2, since it counts double in the Writing score.
- Friday: Light day, review of the error log, and rest.
- Saturday: One longer block, such as a full section under test conditions.

Adjust the days to your own rhythm. If your weekend falls differently, move the blocks.

## Step 3: Match tasks to energy

Put demanding work in your best hours. For some people that is early morning, for others late evening. Use the tired slots for lighter jobs like vocabulary, shadowing audio, or reading sample answers.

## Step 4: Put review inside the plan

Practice without review is mostly wasted effort. Reserve a slot, even 20 minutes, for checking errors and updating your log. A common split is about two-thirds new practice and one-third review. If you notice you are always skipping review, shrink the practice to make room for it.

## Step 5: Add a buffer

Leave one open slot each week with no fixed task. It catches whatever slipped: a missed session, a section that needs another pass, or a day lost to load-shedding. Without a buffer, one bad day leaves the whole schedule broken.

## Step 6: Review the plan every week

At the end of the week, spend ten minutes asking:

- Which sessions did I actually do?
- Which skill got too little time?
- What did the error log say?
- What will I change next week?

Small changes beat dramatic rewrites. If you keep missing an evening session, move it to the morning rather than blaming yourself.

## Plan toward your test date

If your exam date is fixed, work backwards. Early weeks can focus on building skills and question types. Later weeks should add more timed sections and full tests. In the last week, ease off new material, check your exam centre location and the ID you must bring, and protect your sleep.

A schedule is a tool, not a verdict. It cannot guarantee a result, but it does make sure that every skill is touched, every error is reviewed, and your effort goes where it is needed.

Try this week: draw your fixed commitments on paper, fill in one task per study slot using the pattern above, and add a single buffer slot. On the weekend, review what worked and edit the plan.

title: Moving from Band 6 to Band 7 in Writing: what actually changes
excerpt: Band 6 and Band 7 essays often look similar at a glance. The gap sits in a few specific habits, and each one can be practised.
body:
Many of us reach Band 6 in Writing fairly quickly and then stay there for months. The essays are complete, the grammar is mostly fine, the vocabulary is decent. So what is missing? Usually it is not one big thing. It is four small things that the examiner sees across the whole script.

Writing is marked on four criteria: Task Achievement (Task 1) or Task Response (Task 2), Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range and Accuracy. Let us go through what tends to separate a safe 6 from a 7.

## Answer the whole question, and commit to a position

A common Band 6 pattern is an essay that discusses the topic but does not fully answer the question asked. If the prompt says "to what extent do you agree", the examiner wants a clear position from the introduction to the conclusion. A Band 7 response keeps that position visible and develops its main ideas with some depth, rather than listing many ideas in one line each.

Fix: before writing, spend two minutes on a plan. Write your position in one sentence, then two main ideas, each with a reason and a short example. Two well-developed paragraphs beat four thin ones.

## Make paragraphs do one job

Band 6 writers often use linking words correctly but mechanically: "Firstly", "Moreover", "In addition" at the start of every sentence. Band 7 is about logical flow. Each paragraph has a clear central idea, and the sentences inside it connect through reference and logic, not only through connectors.

Fix: write a topic sentence for every body paragraph, then check that each following sentence explains, gives a reason or gives an example for it. If a sentence does none of these, cut it.

## Vocabulary: precision over decoration

We often try to impress with rare words and end up with unnatural phrases. Band 7 shows a flexible, fairly precise vocabulary with some less common items used with awareness of style and collocation. A few errors are acceptable, but the word choice must feel intentional.

- Replace vague words (things, good, bad, many people) with specific ones that fit the topic.
- Learn words in collocations, not alone: "pose a threat", "place a strain on", not just "threat" and "strain".
- Use a word only if you could write a correct sentence with it from memory.

## Grammar: range plus control

For Band 7 you need a variety of complex structures and frequent error-free sentences. Many Band 6 scripts have complex sentences, but too many of them contain errors, so the examiner cannot give credit. The answer is not to avoid complex grammar. It is to use a small set of structures you control well: relative clauses, conditionals, passive forms and concession ("Although... ").

Then proofread for your own habitual mistakes. Most of us repeat the same three or four: articles, subject-verb agreement, plurals, tense shifts. Keep a personal error list and check for exactly those in the last few minutes.

## Task 1 is not a smaller Task 2

For Task 1, remember it needs 150+ words and a clear overview of the main trends or features. Band 6 reports often list every number without selecting. A Band 7 report highlights key features, makes comparisons, and gives an overview paragraph. Task 2 needs 250+ words and counts double toward the Writing score, so protect your time: roughly 20 minutes for Task 1 and 40 for Task 2.

## Practise with feedback, not just volume

Writing ten essays without feedback often repeats the same errors ten times. Write one essay, check it against the four criteria, then rewrite the weakest paragraph. That rewrite is where band movement happens. No one can promise a band score from a method, but this is a reliable way to find what is holding yours back.

Try this week: Take one Task 2 essay you wrote earlier. Underline your position in the introduction and conclusion, rewrite one thin body paragraph with a reason and a specific example, and list the three grammar errors you repeat most. Keep that list beside you for your next essay.

title: Speaking mistakes that keep learners at Band 5.5, and what to do instead
excerpt: Short answers, memorised scripts and long hesitations are common reasons for a Speaking plateau. Here is what to change in each part of the test.
body:
The Speaking test lasts 11 to 14 minutes and has three parts. In that short time the examiner listens for four things: fluency and coherence, lexical resource, grammatical range and accuracy, and pronunciation. When learners stay around 5.5, the cause is usually a handful of habits, not a lack of English. The good news is that habits can change.

## Mistake 1: answers that are too short

In Part 1, many of us answer in one sentence: "Yes, I like cooking." That is correct but gives the examiner almost nothing to assess. At this level, the examiner needs to hear you extend an idea.

Instead: answer, add a reason, add a small example. "I enjoy cooking, mostly on weekends, because during the week I come home late from work and there is no time. Last Friday I made khichuri for my family." Two to three sentences is a good target for Part 1.

## Mistake 2: long pauses while searching for the perfect word

Silence is natural for a moment. But frequent long pauses to find an exact word break fluency. Some learners also repeat the same word or phrase again and again to fill time.

Instead: learn to rephrase. If you forget the word, describe it: "the thing you use to... ". Also practise short natural fillers such as "Let me think", "Well, to be honest", used lightly, not in every sentence.

## Mistake 3: memorised answers

Memorised answers are easy to notice. The rhythm changes, the speed jumps, and the answer may not fit the question. Examiners are trained to recognise this, and it can hurt your assessment because it does not show your real language ability.

Instead: memorise ideas, not sentences. For common topics (hometown, study, work, technology), prepare two or three real stories and the vocabulary around them, then speak freshly each time.

## Mistake 4: simple grammar only, or complex grammar with many errors

At 5.5, we often stay inside "I think... because... " all the time, or try long sentences and lose control.

Instead: add one or two controlled structures per answer. Use past and present together ("I used to... but now I... "), a simple conditional ("If I had more time, I would... "), or a contrast ("Although it is expensive, ... ").

## Mistake 5: ignoring pronunciation features beyond single sounds

Many learners work on individual sounds only. Examiners also listen to word stress, sentence stress and intonation. Flat, rushed speech is harder to follow even when the words are right.

Instead: record yourself, listen back, and mark the words you want to stress. Slow down slightly. Clear, steady speech is better than fast, unclear speech.

## Mistake 6: Part 2 running out of ideas

For the long turn you get a minute to prepare and then speak for up to two minutes. A common problem is stopping at 40 seconds.

Instead: use the preparation minute to note keywords only, not sentences. Cover what happened, where, who, and how you felt, then explain why it mattered. If you finish early, the examiner may ask a question, but do not depend on it.

## Mistake 7: Part 3 answers that stay personal

Part 3 asks for more abstract discussion: society, trends, causes, comparisons. Answers like "I like it" are too thin.

Instead: step back from "I" to "people" or "young people in Bangladesh". Give an opinion, a reason, and a comparison between past and present or between groups.

## A practice routine that fits a busy week

You do not need two hours. Choose one question, answer for one minute on your phone, listen once, and note two things to improve. On a Dhaka commute you can even do the thinking part silently and record later. Because Speaking is judged on how you sound, listening to yourself is the most useful habit we know.

Try this week: Record yourself answering five Part 1 questions. For each answer, check whether you gave a reason and an example. Re-record the two weakest answers, and compare the two versions.

title: How to stop panicking in the Reading section
excerpt: Sixty minutes, forty questions and no extra time can make anyone's heart race. A calm plan, practised in advance, matters more than reading faster.
body:
Almost all of us have had this moment: ten minutes into Passage 1, we realise we have answered only three questions, and the clock suddenly feels louder. Panic makes us reread the same lines, and the more we reread, the less we remember. Reading panic is usually a process problem, not a language problem, so it can be improved with a plan.

## Know the numbers

The Academic Reading test has 40 questions over three passages in 60 minutes. There is no extra time at the end to copy answers to a separate sheet, so you must write your answers as you go. Passages tend to get more demanding as you progress, which is why many learners plan roughly 20 minutes per passage and keep Passage 3 from being rushed.

Treat 20 minutes as a guide, not a rule. The point is that you have a number in your head, so you notice early when you are falling behind.

## Do not read every word first

Reading the whole passage slowly before looking at the questions feels safe, but it burns time. A better routine for most question types:

- Spend a minute on the title, headings and first lines of paragraphs to see the structure.
- Read the questions and underline keywords.
- Scan for those keywords or their synonyms, then read carefully around them.

You are looking for evidence, not trying to enjoy the article.

## Have a skip rule

Panic often begins on one hard question. Decide in advance: if a question has taken more than about a minute and a half, mark it, guess if you wish, and move on. There is no penalty for a wrong answer in IELTS, so never leave a blank. Coming back with fresh eyes often makes the answer obvious.

## Handle unknown words calmly

Academic passages contain words we have never seen. Most of the time you do not need them. Ask: is this word inside the sentence that holds my answer? If not, ignore it. If yes, use the surrounding words and the word's parts to guess the general meaning.

## Control your body first

Panic is physical. When you notice it, stop for five seconds, put both feet flat on the floor, drop your shoulders and breathe out slowly. It sounds small, but it breaks the loop of racing thoughts. Practise this during your mock tests so it is automatic on test day.

## Build calm through mock conditions

Confidence comes from repetition under the same conditions. Do full timed passages, with no pausing, no phone and no dictionary. If load-shedding or a noisy house makes quiet study hard, a library, an early morning slot or earphones can help. After each practice, review your time per passage and your error types, not just your score. Over a few weeks you will see patterns: maybe True/False/Not Given costs you the most time, or matching headings.

## A note on Not Given and Matching

Two question types cause many panic spirals. For True/False/Not Given, decide only from what the passage says, not from what you know. For matching headings, read the paragraph for its main idea, not for a single matching word. A clear method for each type saves minutes.

## On the day

Arrive early, because travel delays in Dhaka are common and stress from rushing carries into the test. Bring the documents your centre requires. Once the paper opens, take one breath, then begin with the passage as planned. If you notice panic returning, use the five-second reset and go back to the next question.

Try this week: Do one timed passage with a 20-minute limit. Mark every question that took more than a minute and a half, and note why: unknown vocabulary, question type, or simply losing focus. Pick one cause and practise only that next time.

title: Why Listening scores stall, and how to break through
excerpt: If your Listening score has stayed the same for weeks, more practice tests may not be the answer. Reviewing your mistakes carefully usually is.
body:
A Listening score that does not move can feel unfair, especially if we are doing a test every day. But doing more tests and getting better are different things. The Listening test is about 30 minutes, with 40 questions across four sections, and the audio is played once. That single hearing is why small gaps in habit show up so clearly in the score.

## Reason 1: we check the score and stop there

Many learners finish a test, count the correct answers, feel disappointed or relieved, and open the next one. The learning is in the mistakes. Each wrong answer has a cause, and until you know the cause, you will repeat it.

Fix: for every wrong answer, listen again with the transcript and sort the error into one type:

- I did not hear the word (sound problem).
- I heard it but misspelled it.
- I heard it but chose the wrong option because of a distractor.
- I lost my place and missed it.
- I did not understand the vocabulary.

After five tests you will see which category is largest. That is your real problem.

## Reason 2: we only listen passively

Listening to podcasts or videos helps, but passive listening alone rarely fixes specific weaknesses. Dictation does. Take a short clip of 20 to 30 seconds, write exactly what you hear, then compare with the transcript. The words you missed show what your ear cannot yet catch: weak forms, linked sounds, numbers, names.

## Reason 3: distractors

IELTS speakers often correct themselves: "Thursday... no, sorry, Friday". The first answer is mentioned but is not the final one. If we write the first thing we hear, we lose the mark.

Fix: write only after the speaker has finished the point. Listen for correction signals like "actually", "sorry", "I mean" and "on second thought".

## Reason 4: spelling and small details

A correct word with wrong spelling gets no mark. Plurals, singulars, and common words like "accommodation" or "Wednesday" are easy places to lose points. Numbers, dates and letters read aloud (especially names and postcodes) also need practice.

Fix: keep a list of words you misspelled, and revise it weekly. Practise writing numbers and letters while listening.

## Reason 5: not using the preview time

Before each section you get a short time to read the questions. Learners who spend it only waiting lose an advantage. Use it to underline keywords, predict the type of answer (a number, a name, a place) and notice the order of questions, which follows the audio.

## Reason 6: unrealistic practice conditions

Listening on the phone in a noisy bus, or with an earphone in one ear, builds habits that do not match the exam room. At least a few times a week, practise in real conditions: full test, single play, no pausing. If power cuts or noise are a problem at home, use early morning hours or a quiet spot at a library or office.

## Reason 7: accents

The test includes a range of accents. If you only practise with one, others will feel difficult. Add short clips from British, Australian, Canadian and other English speakers to your routine.

## Building a simple weekly pattern

Plan something small and repeatable. For example: two full sections per week, one dictation session of 15 minutes, and one mistake review. This is more useful than three tests with no review. Over several weeks, the pattern of errors changes, and that is the sign that you are improving. No one can promise a score from a method, but a clear review habit is how stalled scores usually start moving.

Try this week: Take one section you have already done. Re-listen with the transcript, label each wrong answer with one of the five error types above, and write down your most common type. Practise only that type for the next seven days.

title: The Last 48 Hours Before Your IELTS Test
excerpt: Two days out, the best thing you can do is protect your sleep, sort your documents and stop cramming. Here is a calm checklist that works around Dhaka traffic and load-shedding.
body:
By the time you reach the last two days, most of your score is already decided. What remains is protecting what you have built. We have seen learners lose focus on test day not because of weak English, but because of a missing document, a two-hour commute they did not plan for, or a night of cramming that left them blank at the Listening section.

## Two days before: sort the logistics

Start with your documents. Take out the passport you used when booking, because the ID you present must match your registration. Check that it is the original and in good condition, and read your booking confirmation for the exact date, time and venue. If anything does not match, contact the test centre or your booking agent today, not tomorrow morning.

Then plan the journey. If the centre is across Dhaka or in another city, do the route in your head or, better, visit the area. Think about the traffic at the hour you will travel, and add a generous buffer. Many of us underestimate how long a rickshaw, CNG or bus takes when the roads jam. If you have to travel the evening before, arrange a place to stay with people you trust rather than a long early-morning trip.

Prepare a simple bag:

- Passport and a printed or saved copy of your booking details
- A water bottle if the centre allows it, and a light snack for after
- Clothes in layers, since exam rooms can be cold or warm
- Cash for transport, and a charged phone left switched off or stored as instructed

Leave anything the centre prohibits at home. Check the rules in your confirmation so you are not surprised at the door.

## The day before: lighten the load

Study lightly. Do one short review session: skim your error log, reread two or three model answers, and say your Part 2 outline for a topic or two aloud. Do not attempt a full mock test the day before. A bad score in a rushed practice can shake your confidence for no useful reason.

Keep your meals normal. This is not the day to try a new restaurant or a very spicy dish. Drink enough water, and keep tea or coffee at your usual level so you do not get headaches or jitters.

## Sleep is part of your preparation

Aim to go to bed at a reasonable hour on both nights, and wake up at the time you will need on test day. If load-shedding is common in your area, charge your phone and a torch, keep a hand fan nearby, and set two alarms, one on a different device. Do not rely on one alarm that depends on power.

If you cannot fall asleep the night before, do not panic. One restless night rarely ruins a test, especially if the previous night was decent. Lie quietly, breathe slowly, and rest anyway.

## What to avoid

- Late-night cramming of new vocabulary lists
- Comparing your plan with friends who sound more confident
- Reading forums about difficult tests
- Changing your essay structure or speaking approach at the last minute
- Heavy physical exertion or a long night out

## On the morning

Eat something you know agrees with you. Leave earlier than you think you need to. Arrive calm, not rushed, and take a few slow breaths before entering. If something goes wrong, tell the invigilator or staff politely and early.

Try this week: write your own one-page test-day checklist now, covering documents, route, bag, meals and alarms, and tick it off two days before your real test.

title: Computer-Delivered vs Paper-Based IELTS: What to Practise Differently
excerpt: The content and band scale are the same, but the way you answer is not. Here is how to adjust your practice depending on which format you booked.
body:
Both formats test the same four skills and use the same band scale. The questions are written to the same standard, so a strong learner can do well in either. But the experience of answering differs, and small habits that are fine on paper can cost you on a screen, and the other way round. The first step is simple: know which format you booked, then practise in that format at least some of the time.

## Listening

On paper, you write answers on the question booklet as you listen, then you get time at the end to transfer them to the answer sheet. On the computer, you type answers directly, and the final review time is much shorter. Check the current official instructions for exact timings, because they matter here.

What this means for practice:

- On paper, practise transferring neatly and quickly, with spelling and plural forms checked.
- On computer, type as you listen. Practise your typing speed, since slow typing means missed audio.
- On both, never leave a blank. A guess costs nothing.

Spelling counts in both formats, so keep a list of words you often misspell.

## Reading

You have 60 minutes for 40 questions in both formats, and there is no extra time to transfer answers. On paper, you can underline, circle and write on the passage. On the computer, you usually get highlighting and note tools, but you scroll and navigate between text and questions, which feels different.

If you are taking the computer test, do at least a few Reading practice tests on a laptop or desktop. Check that you are comfortable with scrolling, moving between passages and tracking your time on a screen. If you are taking paper, keep practising with a pen and printed passages, as many of us already do.

## Writing

Task 1 needs at least 150 words and Task 2 at least 250 words, and Task 2 counts double, so protect your time for it. On paper, handwriting must be clear enough to read. Cross-outs are fine, but messy pages slow the examiner and you. On computer, you type, and a word counter is usually available, which saves counting lines.

For paper candidates, practise handwritten essays under timed conditions, and check that your hand does not tire in 60 minutes. For computer candidates, practise typing full essays without relying on spellcheck, because it will not be there. Learn to plan on the provided scratch paper, then type cleanly. Typing makes editing easier, but also tempts us to rewrite sentences too much and run out of time.

## Speaking

Speaking is a face-to-face conversation with an examiner in both formats, usually lasting 11 to 14 minutes. Nothing about the format changes how you answer. Practise speaking aloud in either case.

## Build your plan

1. Confirm your format and read its official guidance.
2. Use at least two full mock tests under the real conditions: pen and paper, or screen and keyboard.
3. After each mock, note format-specific mistakes separately from English mistakes: slow typing, lost place on screen, messy handwriting, or answer-sheet errors.
4. Do not change your English study just because the format changed. The skills are the same.

Many learners in Bangladesh use a phone for most study, which makes keyboard practice even more important. A laptop session twice a week is enough to build comfort.

Try this week: do one timed Reading or Writing practice in the exact format you will sit, and write down three small habits you need to fix.

title: How to Read Your Feedback and Turn It into Next Week's Plan
excerpt: Feedback only helps if it changes what you do on Monday. Here is a simple way to read AI or teacher comments and turn them into a small, realistic study plan.
body:
We often read feedback once, feel good or bad about the band, and move on. Then next week's practice looks exactly like last week's. The comments contain a plan, but only if we sit with them for ten minutes and ask the right questions.

## Start with the criteria, not the band

Writing and Speaking are each marked on four criteria. In Writing these are Task Achievement or Task Response, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range and Accuracy. In Speaking they are Fluency and Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy, and Pronunciation. An overall band hides which of these is pulling you down.

Write the four criteria on a page. Next to each, copy the feedback you received, in your own words. You will usually find that one or two criteria hold you back more than the others.

## Look for patterns, not single mistakes

One missed article is a slip. The same article error in six sentences is a pattern. When we read feedback, we should ask:

- Which mistake appears more than once?
- Which comment did I see in a previous piece of feedback too?
- Which feedback quotes my actual words, and which is general advice?

Specific comments that point to your own sentences or answers are more useful than general tips. If feedback is vague, ask your teacher for an example, or compare it with your own response and check the claim yourself. AI feedback can be wrong or too generous, so treat it as a second opinion, not a verdict. Where a comment does not match what you actually wrote or said, trust your own evidence and check with a teacher.

## Choose one or two priorities

The temptation is to fix everything. Resist it. Pick one priority for the criteria that costs you the most, and a second smaller one. For example:

- Task Response: your Task 2 essays answer only half of the question. Priority: underline every part of the prompt before planning.
- Coherence: paragraphs have no clear main idea. Priority: write one topic sentence per paragraph first.
- Fluency: you stop for long pauses in Part 2. Priority: practise speaking for two minutes on a cue card with a short outline.

## Turn each priority into a small task

A good weekly task is specific, short and testable. Instead of improve grammar, write three Task 2 introductions using a correct paraphrase and a clear opinion, then check them against a model. Instead of better pronunciation, record yourself reading a short paragraph, listen once, and note two sounds or stress patterns to repeat.

A realistic schedule matters. If you work or study during the day, forty focused minutes on four weekdays and a longer session on Friday or Saturday may be more reliable than a big plan you abandon on Tuesday.

## Check whether it worked

At the end of the week, redo a similar task and compare. Did the pattern appear less often? If yes, keep going or move to the next priority. If not, change the method, not just the effort. Perhaps you need a model answer, a teacher's correction, or a different kind of exercise.

Keep an error log: date, mistake, correction, and one new example sentence. After a month, you will see your real progress, which a single band score cannot show.

Try this week: take your latest feedback, choose one priority, write one small task for it, and book the exact time you will do it.

title: Test Anxiety and Speaking to an Examiner for the First Time
excerpt: Nerves are normal, and an examiner is not trying to trick you. Here is how to prepare your body and your answers so the Speaking test feels more like a conversation.
body:
Many of us have practised Speaking alone, with a recording app, or with a friend, but never with a stranger in a quiet room who is writing while we talk. That is a big change, and a racing heart is a normal response. The aim is not to remove nerves completely. It is to make them manageable so they do not take over your English.

## What the Speaking test actually is

The test is a face-to-face conversation of about 11 to 14 minutes with one examiner, and it is recorded. It has three parts. Part 1 is introduction and short questions on familiar topics. Part 2 gives you a cue card, a short time to prepare, and then you speak on your own. Part 3 is a longer discussion on more abstract ideas linked to the topic.

Knowing the structure removes a lot of fear, because you know what happens next. The examiner follows a set format and is trained to be neutral. They may not smile much or react to your answers. That is not a bad sign. They are not judging you as a person.

## Prepare your body first

Anxiety is physical before it is mental. Try these:

- Breathe in for four seconds and out for six, a few times, while waiting outside.
- Relax your shoulders and unclench your hands.
- Drink some water before you go in, if the centre allows.
- Speak slightly slower than feels natural. Nerves make us rush.

## Practise in conditions that feel real

Speaking to a mirror is not enough. Find a friend, cousin, teacher or study partner who will sit across from you, ask questions you have not seen, and not interrupt. Even better, ask someone you do not know well. Record the session and listen later. You will usually notice that you sounded better than you felt.

Practise the opening too: walk in, greet the examiner, say your name, and answer the ID questions. A calm start sets the tone for the next ten minutes.

## Handle moments of blankness

Everyone freezes sometimes. Prepare a few natural phrases:

- That is an interesting question. Let me think for a moment.
- What I mean is...
- Let me put it another way.

If you do not understand a question, you may ask the examiner to repeat it. If you make a mistake, correct it briefly and move on, as native speakers do. Dwelling on it costs more than the mistake did.

## Do not memorise scripts

Learned answers often sound unnatural, and examiners are trained to notice them. Instead, prepare ideas and a few useful words for common topics such as home, work, study, technology, and travel. Give real answers with a reason or a short example, drawn from your own life in Bangladesh, such as your commute, your family, or your city.

## Keep a wider view

One test is one performance on one day. If it goes badly, you can retake it. Thinking this way lowers the pressure, which often improves the performance. Also, a few mistakes do not decide a band; examiners consider your overall language across the whole test.

## The night before and the morning of

Sleep well, eat something light, and arrive early. Waiting is often the hardest part, so bring nothing to study. Think of the first question, take a breath, and begin.

Try this week: do two ten-minute practice interviews with a person, not a recording app, then write down one thing you did well and one habit to change.
